For several NLP tasks, such as answering general knowledge questions, there is a factual or correct response that is generally accepted. However, for some tasks, the “truth” depends on the context or individual interpretation. Consider, for example, the task of determining whether an online comment is offensive. There is no universally agreed notion of offensiveness or hate speech (Vidgen et al., 2019; Fortuna et al., 2020; Leonardelli et al., 2021; Khurana et al., 2022). Instead, the sociocultural background and experiences of the readers influence their judgments (Sap et al., 2022; Goyal et al., 2022). Similarly, judgments depend on a personal interpretation in many other tasks such as for natural language inference (Pavlick and Kwiatkowski, 2019; Nie et al., 2020), semantic annotation (Sommerauer et al., 2020), and understanding indirect *Equal contribution. Not All Subjectivity Is the Same! Defining Desiderata for the Evaluation of Subjectivity in NLP Urja Khurana , Michiel van der Meer *, Enrico Liscio ∗, Antske Fokkens Pradeep K. Murukannaiah Department of Intelligent Systems, Delft University of Technology Leiden Institute of Advanced Computer Science (LIACS), Leiden University Computational Linguistics and Text Mining Lab, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam {u.khurana, e.liscio, p.k.murukannaiah}@tudelft.nl, m.t.van.der.meer@liacs.leidenuniv.nl, antske.fokkens@vu.nl answers (Damgaard et al., 2021). We refer to such tasks that have multiple plausible labels rather than a single valid ground-truth as subjective. As language models are integrated into societal applications, they increasingly engage with subjective concepts such as values, norms, and arguments (Forbes et al., 2020; Lourie et al., 2021; Liscio et al., 2023; Van Der Meer et al., 2024b). Therefore, their behavior must align with varying human preferences (Sorensen et al., 2024) and reflect multiple viewpoints (Cabitza et al., 2023; Plank, 2022). Yet, such models have been shown to collapse to a specific view (Hayati et al., 2024), typically as a consequence of how labels are presented (aggregated to a single majority label) or due to prevalent preference-tuning paradigms (such as RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022) and DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023)) that optimize for the majority vote or general preference (Casper et al., 2023). Obfuscating minority or diverging viewpoints is problematic when deploying models in real-world settings, running the risk of further disenfranchising marginalized communities (Xu et al., 2021). Subjectivity-sensitive models reflect variation in judgment and enable the representation of minority perspectives. As the NLP field pushes for such models (Ovesdotter Alm, 2011; Basile et al., 2021; Plank, 2022; Cabitza et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025), a critical look at their evaluation practices is necessary. Several aspects affect the evaluation of subjectivity-sensitive models, including the ideals we outline, the extent to which subjective evaluation metrics capture overall trends or fine-grained model behavior (Chen et al., 2024; Rizzi et al., 2024), and the type of task (classification vs. generation). To this end, we address the following question: which aspects of subjectivity should evaluation metrics capture? To address this question, we first review how subjectivity is represented in the data and incorporated into NLP models, highlighting a previously 1

These insights further drive our top-down approach, in which we propose a set of sequential desiderata to evaluate subjectivitysensitive models (outlined in Figure 1). We identify aspects not yet addressed in the literature by drawing on insights from related fields. Finally, we map these desiderata onto current evaluation practices, revealing gaps and opportunities for future work. Our key contributions are threefold: (1) the desiderata for evaluating subjectivity-sensitive models, (2) the systematic categorization of current evaluation metrics, and (3) the gaps and opportunities we identify. 2 Subjectivity in Data To establish a fitting evaluation paradigm, we start by describing how subjectivity and related concepts are interpreted in the NLP field. Next, we discuss what the sources of subjectivity are. Finally, we reflect on the types of information to incorporate in a subjectivity-sensitive dataset. 2.1 Subjectivity and Related Concepts Subjectivity pertains to the existence of multiple valid ground-truths (Vardomskaya, 2018; Rottger et al., 2022; Plank, 2022). NLP literature also discusses other concepts related to subjectivity. Perspectivism (Cabitza et al., 2023; Frenda et al., 2025) recognizes that the ground-truth depends on individual perspectives. This has taken shape in the form of a perspectivist framework that enables representing different perspectives in data; weak when taking multiple perspectives into account only during the annotation stage and strong when extending this to incorporating multiple perspectives in the model output as well. Subjective interpretations can lead to disagreement (Uma et al., 2021b) when different individuals have opposing views on a specific input. Plank (2022) uses the term human label variation to refer to instances with different plausible perspectives, since disagreement Depends on the context; opinions vary! Disagreement can also arise in factual matters. This captures annotator errors, either from misunderstanding (genuine misinformation or misinterpreting explicit annotation guidelines) or attention drifts during annotation. 2.2 Sources of Subjectivity Where do multiple viewpoints or beliefs that lead to disagreement stem from? Aroyo and Welty (2015) suggest three potential sources of subjectivity in their Triangle of Reference framework that maps out the process of interpreting an input: task ambiguity, input ambiguity, and annotator attitude.1 Task Ambiguity. Imprecise task definitions and annotation guidelines may (un)intentionally leave enough space for an annotator to fill the gaps through their own interpretation (Rottger et al., 2022). For instance, in “Berlin decided ...”, the entity Berlin can be annotated as location or organization. Without explicitly guiding annotators in such scenarios (in this case, where a city name is used to refer to a government), unintended disagreement can arise. Precise guidelines can still leave some room for personal interpretation, e.g., in Natural Language Inference where implications are debatable or in hate speech where severity is a personal judgment. Input Ambiguity. Even when the task is clearly defined, an input can still warrant multiple interpretations, e.g., when more context is needed to make an accurate judgment. Consider an input that contains a reclaimed slur; determining whether it is hate speech or not requires the knowledge of who is behind the piece of text. Annotator Attitude. Factors such as an annotator’s demographic, emotional state, and experience can yield different valid judgments (Sap et al., 1We adopt the terminology for these three sources from Jiang and de Marneffe (2022) and Liu et al. (2023). 2

2022). This is particularly the case when there is no universally agreed upon ground-truth. 2.3 Incorporating Subjectivity in Data To train and evaluate models that can handle subjectivity, adequate datasets should be available. The conventional approach to building datasets in NLP is to collect n annotations per sample and aggregate them into a single “gold” label, e.g., through majority voting. However, when there is variation in annotator response, this results in a loss of information on human disagreement. This has led to calls for the release of raw annotations (Prabhakaran et al., 2021; Cabitza et al., 2023; Pandita et al., 2025), with recent work showing the importance of having a large number of annotations per sample (Khurana et al., 2024; Gruber et al., 2024). Annotators. Beyond the raw annotations, other dimensions are required to model subjectivity effectively. To model the opinion of a specific individual, for each annotator we would need demographic information (Bender and Friedman, 2018; Prabhakaran et al., 2021) and a sufficient amount of annotated samples. Moreover, disagreement can also stem from annotation mistakes (e.g., due to attention drift), requiring methods (Gordon et al., 2021; Weber-Genzel et al., 2024; Jinadu and Ding, 2024; Ivey et al., 2025) and metrics (Abercrombie et al., 2025) that can distinguish such noise from actual signal. Dumitrache et al. (2018) introduce metrics that capture inter-annotator disagreement in annotation, taking into account the interdependency of the sources of subjectivity. Annotator Population. Raw annotations and annotator information are especially valuable when we are strategic about who is annotating. When subjectivity needs to be captured, carrying out the annotation procedure and choosing the appropriate annotator(s) is an essential task. Smarter sample annotation techniques are needed to get a wider picture of how an input is perceived. This could be accomplished either by ensuring that a specific sample is annotated by a variety of demographics (Van Der Meer et al., 2024a) or by selecting annotators of a specific target group (Goyal et al., 2022). Pei and Jurgens (2023) highlight the importance of labeling with a demographically balanced annotator pool. Díaz et al. (2022) advocate for a more thoughtful process by providing a framework for annotation collection that takes into account subjectivity throughout the multiple annotation stages. 3 Dimensions of Subjective Input What do the sources of subjectivity mean for a subjectivity-sensitive model? Where task ambiguity plays an overarching role when collecting ground-truth labels across multiple samples, input ambiguity and annotator attitude can primarily occur at a sample level. These two sources require the model to handle subjectivity differently, an aspect that has not yet been addressed in previous research. We characterize model behavior when dealing with different sources of subjectivity on two dimensions: ambiguity and polyphony (Figure 2). polyphonic Wow, they are such a great community! I hate boomers... ambiguous nonambiguous Exclude those *** from society I will take this b[*/i]tch out monophonic : different perspectives : disambiguations/clarifications : clear ground-truth Figure 2: Dimensions of sources of subjectivity at a sample-level: ambiguity on the x-axis and polyphony on the y-axis. For each quadrant, we show the desired model output (as icons) with an example situated in hate speech detection. When an input is non-ambiguous and monophonic, a model can directly incorporate the objective ground-truth. However, modeling scenarios involving subjective factors is more challenging as the following subsections illustrate. 3.1 Ambiguous ↔Non-Ambiguous An input is ambiguous when it can warrant different interpretations because the information (e.g., context) needed to make a judgment is incomplete. Inputs that can be interpreted without filling information gaps are non-ambiguous. Ambiguous. When faced with an ambiguous input, a model should identify the spectrum of different possible interpretations and disambiguations. For instance, in “I will take this b{*/i}tch out” the ambiguity lies in who the b-word refers to; the slur or the dog. In a multi-turn conversation, the model can engage with the user to increase the information needed to resolve ambiguity. When a response 3

[SOURCE PAGE 4 | SECTION introduction]
is directly needed, the model can provide the user with the different possibilities accordingly. Non-ambiguous. A non-ambiguous input removes the requirement for a model to understand the different interpretations. In such a situation, the model can directly give a suitable response based on the exact information outlined in the input. 3.2 Polyphonic ↔Monophonic Independent of ambiguity, certain inputs may not have an agreed-upon ground truth, allowing for judgments based on an individual’s interpretation. Personal taste, demographics, background, experience, and other factors influence this interpretation. We consider such cases to be polyphonic: different perspectives co-existing. Where there is unanimity, we consider that to be monophonic. Polyphonic. A polyphonic input is open to multiple valid perspectives, which the model should capture. Take for example the statement “I hate boomers”; the meaning is clear but the polyphony lies in whether boomers are considered targets of hate speech. A model that can capture polyphony for the right reasons will be able to generalize well in the real world. Thus, the model should recognize what aspect(s) of the input enable different perspectives and why, e.g., is it the gender or culture that potentially influences the opinion or are there other factors? Not every different perspective has to be attributed to specific demographics, certain deviations can also be due to individual differences. Monophonic. When an input has a single valid belief, often connected to factuality, the model can directly predict the ground-truth without the need to consider a variety of potential perspectives. For instance, the phrase “Exclude those *** from society” should not warrant any subjective interpretation due to its overt form of hate speech. 3.3 Ambiguous and Polyphonic Ambiguity and polyphony can be intertwined. Consider an input that lacks context and warrants multiple perspectives, e.g., “Wow, they are such a great community”. Here, the ambiguity lies in the sentiment of the sentence and the polyphony in the gravity of the (potential) negative sentiment. In such a scenario, a model is expected to capture the appropriate disambiguation and clarification questions, and the different possible perspectives. 4 Subjectivity in Models How a model expresses subjectivity influences its evaluation. Thus, we discuss ways of expressing and instilling subjectivity in models, considering both classification and free-text generation objectives. 4.1 Expressing Subjectivity To move away from rigid responses in line with the majority preference, the model’s output should reflect the spectrum of different perspectives or be aligned to an individual’s perspective. Spectrum of Perspectives. A model that reflects diverse perspectives and values is pluralistically aligned. Sorensen et al. (2024) map out two operationalizations of pluralistic alignment that reflect a multitude of viewpoints. (1) In the distributional approach, the model outputs the distribution of perspectives in the generated response, allowing the user to be informed of the presence of a variety of other opinions. This can either be expressed in the logits or softmax distribution of the model, or directly in the generated response (Meister et al., 2025). (2) In the overton approach, the generated response summarizes different reasonable perspectives. Determining what is reasonable depends on the individual; thus, it requires (some degree of) personalization. While an autoregressive model would generate a free-text response, an autoencoder can express this through a multi-label setup. Individual Preferences. A model that can tailor its response according to the preferences of an individual or a group (where these preferences are shared) is steerable (Sorensen et al., 2024). The model considers a variety of perspectives and values and steers its response to be closest to the perspective of the user. This is closely related to personalization, where preferences go beyond values and include matters such as textual style or lifestyle (e.g., food or films) (Zhang et al., 2025). 4.2 Instilling Subjectivity We distinguish between approaches that introduce the notion of subjectivity at inference, when training or fine-tuning, and when aligning the models. Inference-time Strategies. Integrating subjectivity at test time is a more computationally efficient solution than training/fine-tuning, particularly in the case of LLMs. A popular approach is persona prompting (Santurkar et al., 2023; Deshpande et al., 4

The persona could either steer the subjectivity toward a specific perspective or provide a spectrum of multiple perspectives. Instead of a persona, we can also retrieve user history (examples relevant to the task of choice) and include it in the prompt using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG; Lewis et al., 2020). The model then uses this history to adapt its response. Used for a variety of personalization tasks (Li et al., 2024; Salemi et al., 2024a,b; Mysore et al., 2024; Richardson et al., 2023), this approach, to our knowledge, has not been applied to pluralistic steering. Training/Fine-tuning. Different approaches have been devised to enable subjective modeling during the fine-tuning stage. The conventional approach is to use soft labels, i.e., the distribution of class annotations for a single sample (Jamison and Gurevych, 2015; Uma et al., 2021a; Fornaciari et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023). Instead of optimizing for a single (aggregated) hard label, the goal is to minimize the distance between the estimated distribution and the actual distribution. This is typically done using distance-based loss functions such as cross-entropy, Kullback Leibler-, or Jensen-Shannon divergence. Another avenue is learning from individual annotators’ labels to make distributional or single predictions (Rodrigues and Pereira, 2018). Strategies for this include fine-tuning on annotator-specific labels (Deng et al., 2023; Hoeken et al., 2025), ensembling over annotator-specific models (Khurana et al., 2024), multi-task settings (Mostafazadeh Davani et al., 2022), and PEFT-based strategies that provide a cheaper solution than fully fine-tuning autoregressive models (Tan et al., 2024; Ignatev et al., 2025). Alignment Methods. Preference tuning methods for large language models are designed primarily to optimize according to the majority preference (Casper et al., 2023). As such, strategies are being developed to create pluralistic alignment methods, i.e., methods that can reflect a multitude of preferences and tailor their responses accordingly (Zhao et al., 2024; Poddar et al., 2024; Jang et al., 2024). 5 Desiderata for Subjective Models After outlining the desired model output when facing a subjective input, the natural next step is to evaluate its performance. But what does it mean for a model to perform well on subjective input? To answer this question, we propose desiderata for a subjectivity-sensitive model. These desiderata are motivated by three overarching ideals rooted in our preceding discussion of how subjectivity is represented in NLP data and models: (1) representation of all, including minority voices, (2) based on the correct sources of subjectivity in the input, and (3) the representation of subjectivity (in data and models) generalizing to the real world. D1. Recognize when subjective modeling is necessary As we highlight in Section 2.1, certain inputs have multiple valid perspectives. For a model to make predictions that reflect this diversity, the first step is to recognize when an input needs to be treated subjectively versus objectively. Even when a task is generally considered to be subjective, this step is vital—there will be cases where raters will have consensus, e.g., when dealing with a severe case of hate speech; predicting an aggregate estimate would be sufficient in that case. D2. Recognize which type of subjective modeling is needed As we describe in Section 3, model behavior depends on the type of subjective input. Thus, a model should recognize which type of subjectivity the input contains: ambiguity, polyphony, or both. D3. Recognize why there is subjectivity in the input Building on the desired model behavior we outline in Section 3, a model should recognize why there is ambiguous or polyphonic subjectivity in the input. Using this information, the model can delineate the different disambiguations, clarifications, or perspectives to resolve. This facilitates better predictions and more reliable generalization to unseen scenarios. D4. Predict subjectivity accurately After recognizing the source of the subjectivity, a model should predict the subjectivity correctly. A 5

Calibrate the output with respect to the frequency of opinions As we illustrate in Section 4.2, certain models are trained to estimate the distribution of human judgment for an input. Depending on how subjectivity is expressed (distributional or overton), the predicted distribution should be calibrated to the actual human judgment distribution. This applies both when a probability distribution is obtained directly from the model and when an overton response is generated. For an overton response, the linguistic quantifiers should be well-calibrated. This also extends to when a model relies on uncertainty metrics to identify whether it has encountered a subjective input. D6. Represent all perspectives A subjectivity-sensitive model should account for the minority voices that are usually lost in aggregation. The model should represent a range of diverse viewpoints, minimizing bias toward dominant perspectives. Relevant perspectives should be decoupled from dominant perspectives. For example, it should not only echo a Western perspective but also other cultures when the input warrants it. D7. Express subjectivity without hampering user experience A subjectivity-sensitive model carries with it the responsibility of informing a user of different perspectives. This mirrors the responsibility of showing users explanations of decision-making in the field of explainable AI (XAI). What counts as a “good” explanation depends on the user (Ehsan and Riedl, 2020). In a similar vein, we argue that subjectivity should be expressed in a way that does not hamper user experience. Consider a model giving a summary of all the different perspectives. It is of limited use when a response enumerates all potential perspectives,2 making it rather infeasible to grasp the overall view. Here, it should strike a balance between being concise and detailed according to user preference. 2Note that this excludes the setting where the output of the model is distributional. Note that the model does not have to be explicitly designed to address all of the desiderata, but can capture them implicitly as well (e.g., a model does not have to be explicitly designed to output binary labels for D1, it can cover this desideratum implicitly when directly predicting the human judgment distribution). To what extent all the desiderata should be covered by the model also depends on the application, e.g., for an NLI model doing requirement analysis, D6. Represent all perspectives is not of utmost importance. 6 Subjectivity Evaluation Practices In Section 5, we formulate the desiderata for a subjectivity-sensitive model in a top-down fashion. We review related literature and identify the main metrics and evaluation practices.3 Predicting the full human judgment distribution. Determining whether subjectivity is accurately predicted depends on how the model expresses it. When disagreement is represented through soft labels, the distance between the original disagreement and softmax distribution of the model is measured. Widely used metrics are (variations of) KLdivergence, Jensen-Shannon Divergence, Mean Absolute Error, Wasserstein, or Total Variation Distance (Rizzi et al., 2024). Wasserstein distance is particularly beneficial when working with ordinal labels. To represent whether a single distribution has high or low variation, entropy H is used (Alies et al., 2025). To measure whether the model can capture human disagreement well, Uma et al. (2020) propose measuring the correlation between the entropy of the soft label and the softmax distribution (Hcorr). These metrics work in classification settings but are not applicable when evaluating free-text generated responses. Keeping our desiderata in mind, we highlight some key aspects that have been (partially) unexplored. The desideratum D7.Express is unaddressed. None of the papers in our analysis studies how to express subjectivity to the user without hampering their experience. Effective modeling of subjectivity is of limited value if the outcome is not adequately conveyed to the user. However, this effectiveness is user-specific. As such, we can borrow insights and metrics from other fields, such as Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) (Ehsan and Riedl, 2020; Benjamin et al., 2022), Affective Computing (Kunc et al., 2024), or Computer-Supported Collaborative Work (Lai et al., 2023), to steer the developments of new expression evaluation strategies. Use insights and metrics from adjacent fields to evaluate D7.Express. The desiderata D2.Recognize which and D3.Recognize why are understudied. Recognizing which type of subjectivity (D2) and why the input is subjective (D3) are addressed implicitly through performance-based analyses. For D3, only one paper explicitly evaluates for disambiguations (in NLI). Some papers resort to qualitative analyses through feature-attribution methods. Interpretability or explainability techniques can play a role in identifying key drivers in the input toward the prediction made. We postulate that such methods can be combined with manually annotated data to construct metrics that verify whether the model is making its predictions for the right reasons.5 To study D2, the inherent uncertainty surrounding the input could provide a starting point. Traditionally, neural network uncertainty is decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (Hüllermeier and Waegeman, 2021). Aleatoric uncertainty refers to the uncertainty that lies in the input itself such as inherent ambiguity or noise. Measuring the aleatoric uncertainty of an input can thus help identify ambiguous input. It remains a challenge to measure the uncertainty surrounding the polyphony of an input, and we invite future work to tackle this. Design metrics to address D2.Recognize which and D3.Recognize why, potentially through methodologies for uncertainty estimation and explainability. The entanglement of polyphony and ambiguity has not been at the forefront yet. These two have been studied in isolation. As illustrated in Section 3, the two types of subjectivity can cooccur and understanding how a model handles this interplay can help in gaining broader insights into the model’s sensitivity to subjective input. Study the entanglement of polyphony and ambiguity at a sample-level. A multi-faceted and deployment-driven investigation of model behavior is missing. Taking into account all desiderata is challenging due to limited evaluation practices and experimental constraints. Yet, evaluating models on subjective tasks from a variety of angles is necessary. The impactful nature of NLP models in society demands that these models be sensitive to subjectivity, representing multiple perspectives in their output. We analyze the current evaluation paradigms of subjectivity-sensitive models. We begin by understanding subjectivity and how it is represented in NLP data and models, which leads us to define the desiderata for a subjectivity-sensitive model. We take a top-down approach to design seven desiderata, driven by our ideals for a model to (1) represent all, based on (2) the correct source of subjectivity to (3) generalize to the real world. We then analyze 60 papers to map evaluation metrics to our desiderata. This mapping allows us to identify gaps, which can be fruitful directions for future work. Among these gaps, we primarily find that existing work has overlooked nuances in the types of subjectivity: polyphony versus ambiguity, and we argue that this distinction is crucial for effective evaluation. Additionally, current research efforts do not touch on our seventh desideratum: Express, nor the interplay between different desiderata. We finally highlight the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration to facilitate datasets and annotation strategies that can better capture subjectivity, and in turn, improve subjectivity-sensitive model development and evaluation.
